messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric and Duane,

Thank you so much for your insights, these are very helpful. Yes my problem is the latter, as this was not conducted on trails/roads rather random line transects drawn on a map. We followed all principles of line transect- distance sampling. However, due to the habitat composition of the study area as some were difficult to traverse in a straight line, the transects might have oriented a little further. I corrected the perpendicular distances though, by calculating the distance from the point (we had GPS location) where the prey data was observed to the Euclidean transect (where it supposed to be) by near tool in arcgis and also by compass animal bearing (recorded during the field). So this helped to either add or subtract the distances. Now my rough or data exploration graph looks like the one below.

Am I doing it correctly?

Best wishes,
Samundra

From: Duane Diefenbach <duan...@gmail.com>
Sent: Thursday, August 29, 2024 6:40 PM
To: distance...@googlegroups.com <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Cc: Samundra Subba <samundr...@wwfnepal.org>
Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: How to correct field compass bearing mistakes? A quick query

I would second what Eric suggested. My experience with ungulate distance sampling surveys (white-tailed deer, Odocoileus virginianus). The histogram you shared would be typical for surveys conducted from roads (because deer avoid the areas near roads) or because the survey was conducted on foot and deer were able to detect observers first and move away from the transect line. In the first case (roads as transect), you need independent data to model the distribution of deer relative to the transect (Marques et al. 2013 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10260-012-0223-2). In the second case (deer avoid observers) I'm not sure what you do except modify your data collection methods.

Duane Diefenbach

On Thu, Aug 29, 2024 at 8:22 AM 'Eric Rexstad' via distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> Samundra
>
> There are many reasons that could give rise to the observed distribution of perpendicular distances you show. Most common reasons for this distribution are a) evasive movement on the part of the animals or b) distribution of animals available to be detected is lower at small distances from the transect.  Cause b) is often associated with transects placed along features known to the animals; such as tracks.
>
> If you have eliminated these possible causes, only then can you consider other explanations. Transects need not necessarily be straight, but perpendicular distances do need to be recorded to the transect; this is most easily accomplished with straight transects.
>
> Even if it is correct that compass bearings are at fault, I do not know how you would correct the recorded data. Corrections you might make would also be based upon supposition; thereby introducing new uncertainty into the data.
>
> If the cause of the problem is (b) above, then left truncation is not the remedy. See the short note published by Marques (2016) in response to a paper that employed left truncation in an ungulate survey:
> Marques, T. A. (2016). A comment on Horcajada-Sánchez and Barja (2015): A cautionary tale about left truncation and density gradients in distance sampling. Annales Zoologici Fennici, 53(1/2), 52–54.
>

messages.body_plain:
Yes, Samundra. You want to record the perpendicular distance from the animal to the transect, not distance from animal to observer. Observers might deviate from the transect, but the distance of interest is between the animal and the transect.

Your histogram of detection distances looks reasonable; however, I would carry out truncation of the largest detection distances before fitting detection function models. I cannot read the x-axis scale because the test is small. But I think certainly the last two histogram bars, and perhaps also the third from greatest histogram bar distances might be truncated. The model being fitted is to the process that gives rise to the data (namely the detection process). Beyond some perpendicular distance, detections are influenced more by random chance than by the detection process. These most distant detections are removed such that noise in the data has less influence in the fitted model.

messages.body_plain:
I’m not sure there is much of an issue here. The histogram suggests some avoidance in the first 10 or 12m. If the goodness-of-fit test is not significant, that could be just chance variation and I would ignore it. If the test is significant, it may be that animals move slightly away from the line before detection. If these animals are still being detected, but in the second or third distance interval instead of the first, then the fitted detection function averages out the slight excess of detections in those 2 intervals with the slight shortage in the first interval, and estimation should not really be compromised. Only if many animals on or near the line move and avoid detection altogether might the bias become problematic.

Steve Buckland

I am a PhD student using distance sampling for the first time. I used somewhat unorthodox methods and am hoping for some advice on two quick questions about the best course of action for analysis.

1.  I drove road transects, recording the position of all animals sighted on a map of high-resolution satellite imagery (rather than recording distance and angle to animal). I am aware that this violates some of the typical assumptions of distance sampling. Are there any methods I can use to estimate density that are robust to this approach?
2. Using a laser rangefinder, I estimated the visibility on both sides of the road, every 500 m. Given that my transects are longer than 500 m, I have multiple such measurements per transect. Is there an appropriate way for me to incorporate these visibility measurements into the probability function I will use, given that the visibility taken each 500 m does not precisely represent the visibility at all points along the transect?

Any information would be much appreciated!

Henry

Welcome to the list. As you note, surveys restricted to roads induce bias in your estimates. There are two reasons for this. First, roads are not placed randomly on the landscape, hence they do not provide a representative sample of your study area. If you only want to make inference to the region on either side of the roads, inference to this region might be valid.

Second, your study animal knows about the presence of the road—they are either attracted or repulsed by the presence of the road and associated traffic. In either case, animals are not distributed uniformly at all distances from the road. In this situation, you will need data not only to estimate the shape of the detection function as a function of distance from the road, but you will also need to estimate the shape of the animal availability gradient. Estimating these two functions requires the collection of additional data and cannot be done retrospectively.  Papers below discuss this:

Marques, T. A., Buckland, S. T., Bispo, R., & Howland, B. (2013). Accounting for animal density gradients using independent information in distance sampling surveys. Statistical Methods and Applications, 22, 67–80. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10260-012-0223-2
Marques, T. A., Buckland, S. T., Borchers, D. L., Tosh, D., & McDonald, R. A. (2010). Point transect sampling along linear features. Biometrics, 66, 1247–1255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x
Borchers, D.L. and Cox, M.J. (2017), Distance sampling detection functions: 2D or not 2D?. Biom, 73: 593-602.  https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.12581
Your rangefinder data on visibility will not provide information about animal availability which central to resolving your situation.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Copied below are Eric's comments and suggestions for this analysis and my question

If you are treating year as strata, it is fine if effort differs between years. Imagine your strata were geographic; separating the study area into three geographic pieces. There is no reason that each geographic stratum would have the same amount of effort. Therefore, I don't think your analysis with effort kept the same is reasonable.
Thanks for the spreadsheet. I get the same result as the third page of your Word document from the following code (except your Word document labels the result as a hazard rate when you really fitted a half normal without adjustments):

library(readxl)
isha <- read_xlsx("E:/troubleshoot/Isha/Datasheet.xlsx", sheet = 1)
names(isha)[2] <- "Study.Area"
names(isha)[3] <- "Strata"
names(isha)[5] <- "Area"
names(isha)[7] <- "Region.Label"
names(isha)[10] <- "distance"
names(isha)[15] <- "Effort"

library(Distance)
cu <- convert_units("meter", "kilometer", "square kilometer")
hn5 <- ds(isha, key="hn", adjustment = NULL,
          truncation = "5%", convert_units = cu)
summary(hn5)

I made Effort in the analysis the Yearly.effort column. Hope that makes the analysis clear

Also another point to note, we used a pooled detection function across all years. But Eric's suggestion is to try and compute a separate detection function for all the three years and then compare the models.

I should also mention that the analysis carried out assumes detection probability is constant across years. If detectability does differ between years, the results from that model will be biased.
You should also fit a model with year as a covariate and contrast that AIC with the constant probability model:

library(readxl)

isha <- read_xlsx("E:/troubleshoot/Isha/Datasheet.xlsx", sheet = 1)
names(isha)[2] <- "Study.Area"
names(isha)[3] <- "Strata"
names(isha)[5] <- "Area"
names(isha)[7] <- "Region.Label"
names(isha)[10] <- "distance"
names(isha)[15] <- "Effort"

library(Distance)
cu <- convert_units("meter", "kilometer", "square kilometer")
hn5 <- ds(isha, key="hn", adjustment = NULL,
          truncation = "5%", convert_units = cu)
summary(hn5)

isha$Region.Label <- as.factor(isha$Region.Label)
hn.year.covar <- ds(isha, key="hn",
                    truncation = "5%", convert_units = cu,
                    formula=~Region.Label)

summarize_ds_models(hn5, hn.year.covar)
# You will see that the model with year as a covariate
#          has a considerably smaller AIC

plot(hn.year.covar)

                  lwd=2, lty=1, col="darkred")

                  lwd=2, lty=1, col="darkblue")

                  lwd=2, lty=1, col="darkgreen")
legend("topright", legend=c(2020, 2022, 2023),

Thanks for your question. There could be several causes for the large uncertainty in you estimate of elephant density.

I would suggest you focus upon the variability in encounter rate; differences in detections between cameras.  You note most of your cameras had no detections; I suspect a few of your cameras may have had many detections, resulting in high between-camera variability in encounter rate. Examine your output focusing upon the reported encounter rates and more importantly CV of encounter rate.

I suspect you will find encounter rate is responsible for the majority of uncertainty in your density estimate. That is a common situation with camera trap data. There is considerable small scale heterogeneity in habitats which are manifested in high encounter rate variance.

How do you reduce encounter rate variability? I'm afraid this is an area of current research; I don't have an answer for you. Perhaps researchers who are active in this area and also read these questions might have a suggestion for you.

Please let me know what you think, how you would go about it, or if you would like any clarifications.

Thank you for your help!
All my best,

messages.body_plain:
Welcome Bastien

Conducting distance sampling surveys along trails creates two problems, neither related to curvature of the trails. First, trails are not placed randomly through the habitat, making extrapolation dubious from the vicinity of the trails to the larger area. Second, animals know where the trails are located; they are either attracted or repelled by the trail violating the assumption that animals area evenly distributed with respect to distance from the trail out to the truncation distance.

By combining transects into a single transect, you lose spatial replication hence cannot estimate variability in encounters between transects. This then negates the ability to make inference from the trails to the wider area. But if it is relative change you wish to measure, perhaps you are content with this price to pay. In which case, you can analyse the data in the manner you describe; mindful of the caveats I mentioned.

Monthly surveys over eight years results in nearly 100 months. You might consider combining data across three or four months to increase sample size for each of the surveys.

messages.body_plain:
Nilanjan

It is indeed possible to combine data across years to have adequate data to fit a detection function. However, if you use that pooled detection function to produce year-specific estimates, those estimates will be biased if detectability differs between years.

To avoid this bias, combine data across years, then fit a model that included year as a covariate. This will account for the variability in detectability between years.

An approximate example of this (using species rather than years) can be found here
https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-spec-covar/species-covariate-distill.html
Covariate modeling with rare species <https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-spec-covar/species-covariate-distill.html>

Hope that is useful.

Yes, this can be done using Distance for Windows software. I don't have a ready-made example, but here are some hints.

Organise your data such that years are strata (or regions). Create models where data are stratified, then detection function at the global level (meaning pooled data) and detection function at the stratum level (meaning year-specific detection probabilities). Yasuo

These principles of distance sampling will help guide you in organising your data.

You define a study area about which you want to make inference of population size. Because you define the study area, you know its size. That is the value you provide in the "Area" column.

Into that study area, you randomly place transects, named in the column "Sample.Label" (not "Sample_Label" as you show in the first line of the file you provide). Those transects are of known length (specified by "Effort").

The value of "Area" should be the same for all rows with a given "Region.Label" designation; if not, the error you noted will be generated.

The value of the "Area" field is not computed in the manner  you suggest; it is defined when the study area is delineated.
